title: A bar chart of arms is a claim about a difference: check the baseline, the spread and the scale before believing it
summary: Three Playground figures compare arms of an experiment with bars: normalization arms against a raw baseline, a linear against a nonlinear model on two toy datasets, and three weight-decay settings. Each answers 'which arm is better?', and each is easy to over-read.

media.alt: A dark-background bar chart titled normalization ablation, final test loss by arm, mean plus or minus standard deviation over five seeds. Ten bars: nine cyan normalized arms and one orange raw baseline at the right. Four bars reach the same top height, others are much shorter, and the vertical axis is logarithmic with one labelled tick at 1e5.

read_the_figure.question: Is one arm really better than the baseline, by how much, and could the difference be noise or an artefact of the axis?
read_the_figure.axes: Ablation: horizontal, the arms (names built from the transform, for example min-max or log then min-max, and which variables it is applied to: species, temperature or both); vertical, final test loss in raw units on a log scale. Toy datasets: datasets on the horizontal axis, test accuracy 0 to 1. Weight decay: the three settings (none, l1, l2) against the train-minus-test accuracy gap.
look_at: Orange is the raw baseline; every blue arm is judged against it, not against the other blues.
Error bars show mean plus or minus standard deviation over five seeds. They are barely visible, so seeds agree, but five seeds is a small sample.
Four bars reach exactly the same top height. Equal heights at the edge of the axis usually mean the plot is clipped or the loss hit a ceiling, not that four arms are equally bad by coincidence.
The log axis makes bar length meaningless: on a log scale the bottom of a bar is arbitrary, so compare tops (heights above a gridline) only.
Linear against nonlinear: both reach 1.0 on the Gaussian blobs, the linear model about 0.6 on the circle where classes are nested. The title says exactly that only one dataset is linearly separable.

Weight decay: the vertical value is train accuracy minus test accuracy, so smaller means less overfitting. In this single run l1 is lower than none and l2 is higher, but the differences are about 0.02 to 0.03.
read_the_figure.proves: The toy-dataset figure proves a structural fact (a linear model cannot separate nested classes). The ablation shows that the choice of what to normalize changes final loss by large factors, even with tiny seed spread. The weight-decay figure shows a small difference whose sign cannot be trusted without repeated runs.
if_wrong: A bar that touches the top edge: check whether the axis is clipped before reading its value.
Differences smaller than the plausible noise on test accuracy (a few hundredths for a hundred test points): no conclusion.
A baseline that is not drawn or not in a contrasting colour: the reader cannot tell what 'better' means.
Arms that differ in more than one thing at once: an ablation changes one factor at a time.
must_check: That a baseline arm is present and visibly different.
That error bars are labelled (std or standard error) and the number of seeds stated.
That log axes carry a stated scale and bars are not read by length.
That the metric and its direction are explicit (here loss: lower is better; gap: smaller is less overfitting).

terms.meaning: Remove or change one component and measure what happens, keeping everything else fixed.
The reference arm every other arm is compared with.
A variant that scales inputs or targets with a stated transform before training.
Classes that a straight line (or plane) can split.
A penalty on the size of the weights: l2 uses the sum of squares, l1 the sum of absolute values.
Standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of seeds.

remember: A comparison needs a baseline, a spread over seeds and a stated metric.
On a log axis read bar tops, not bar lengths.
Standard error with n seeds is std / sqrt(n); with five seeds that is std / 2.2.
A linear classifier separates only classes divided by a hyperplane.
A smaller gap does not mean a better model: both accuracies matter.

steps.title: Why the circle defeats a linear model
steps.note: A hyperplane cuts the plane into two half-planes; nested classes need a closed boundary. Adding the feature x1^2 + x2^2 makes the circle linearly separable, which is what a nonlinear model learns.

steps.title: Weight decay as a shrink-then-step update
steps.note: Each update first shrinks the weights by a fixed factor, so large weights must keep earning their size. The l1 version subtracts eta times lambda times sign(w), which drives some weights exactly to zero.

steps.title: Spread of a mean over seeds
steps.note: The error bars in the ablation are standard deviations. The standard error of each mean is about 45 percent of that, so bars that look tight are tighter still for the mean, but five seeds cannot estimate rare failures.

steps.title: Noise floor of an accuracy
steps.note: For p about 0.9 and 100 test points the binomial noise is 0.03. A gap difference of 0.02 to 0.03, as between l1 and none in the figure, is of the same size. The test-set size is not shown; 100 is illustrative.

worked.title: Is the weight-decay difference more than noise?
worked.problem: Gaps read from the figure: none 0.052, l1 0.036, l2 0.084. Assume (illustratively) 100 test points and test accuracy about 0.9. Compare the differences with the binomial noise.

solution.text: Binomial noise on a test accuracy.

worked.answer: Both differences are of the order of the noise (0.03), so this single run does not show that either penalty helps or hurts.

analyze.q: Four bars in the ablation end at the same height. List two explanations and one check for each.
analyze.hint: Clipping versus a genuine ceiling of the loss.

analyze.q: Why does a log axis make bar length a poor encoding? What would you plot instead?
analyze.hint: Dot plot with the baseline as a line.

analyze.q: The weight-decay figure is titled with the hardest dataset. Why does naming the dataset matter for how far the result generalizes?

evaluate.q: Would you adopt the best normalization arm on this evidence? What extra runs do you need?
evaluate.hint: More seeds, another dataset, held-out test.

evaluate.q: Rewrite the claim 'l1 reduces overfitting' so that it is supported by the weight-decay figure.
evaluate.hint: Scope it to the single run and the size of the difference.

create: Redraw the ablation as a dot plot on a log axis with the baseline as a horizontal line and seed values as faint dots.
Design a follow-up that changes only one of the two normalization choices (transform, or which variables) at a time.

checks.q: What does the orange bar mean?
checks.answer: The raw baseline: no normalization; every blue arm is compared with it.

checks.q: Std of 0.3 over five seeds. Standard error?
Why does a linear model score about 0.6 on the circle but 1.0 on the Gaussians?
checks.hint: Which classes are separated by a line?
checks.answer: The Gaussian classes are on opposite sides of a line; the circle classes are nested, so no line can separate them and the best a line can do is a majority-like guess.

checks.q: l2 shows a larger gap than none. Is l2 harmful?
checks.answer: Not demonstrated. The difference is comparable with test-set noise, and the figure has one run and no error bars.

checks.q: Name two additions that would make the ablation figure persuasive.
checks.answer: Several datasets or seeds with intervals, a visible baseline line, and a note on whether any bar is clipped.
